overview: Lenape peoples belong to homelands around the Delaware River and neighboring Atlantic regions. They include distinct Unami and Munsee communities. The imported outline extends well beyond the core homeland; it is not a precise national boundary. Its 1500 to 1650 interval is map coverage, not the lifetime of living Lenape nations.

periods.title: Homelands and community leadership
periods.summary: Related Lenape communities governed themselves through local leaders and family networks.

periods.title: Dispossession and diplomacy
periods.summary: The Walking Purchase accelerated loss of eastern Pennsylvania lands.

periods.title: Treaty diplomacy
periods.summary: Lenape diplomats negotiated a military alliance with the United States.

periods.title: Artistic continuity
periods.summary: Beadwork made in Oklahoma illustrates artistic adaptation after removal.

items.text: Wolf, Turkey and Turtle clans organize important family connections. Delaware Nation explains that clan membership follows the mother’s line and that elders and matriarchs helped select community chiefs. Villages had their own leadership; a shared Lenape identity did not require one ruler over every settlement.

A tribal teaching sheet reconstructs a house with a central fire, roof openings for smoke, and mats insulating the walls. Corn and herbs hang above the living area; food and belongings sit beneath sleeping platforms. Even the ends of the house have jobs, including dry firewood and winter storage.

Food preservation helped gardens last beyond harvest. Corn could be hung up, squash sliced into rings and dried, and meat or fish smoked or dried. Later, water softened dried ingredients for cooking. The pantry therefore depended on sun, smoke and careful work rather than a refrigerator.

One recorded cooking method enclosed a whole fish in clay before baking it in hot ashes. Breaking away the hardened coating also removed skin and scales. The tribal food guide describes a package that helped cook dinner and peel it afterward, an ingenious use of a familiar material.

Spring shad runs drew people together along rivers. A teaching reconstruction shows stakes and weighted nets forming a fish weir, with the catch split and hung near a fire to dry. Fishing was a seasonal harvest requiring construction, timing and food-processing skills as well as catching fish.

Making a dugout canoe meant hollowing a tree trunk without splitting it apart. The tribe’s canoe guide describes controlled burning followed by scraping with an adz; wet hide protected wood that should not burn. Fire helped shape the boat, but only where the builder wanted it.

Language teacher Nora Thompson Dean described a lively football game in 1971. Men who caught the deerskin ball had to stop and kick it onward, while women could run, throw or kick. The ball was stuffed with deer hair. Players needed to know which rules applied to their team!

A museum shoulder bag dated 1740 to 1770 is attributed probably to a Lenape maker. Its deerskin carries porcupine-quill work, metal cones and deer hair. The careful attribution matters: a beautiful surviving object can reveal skilled techniques even when its early collecting history leaves questions.

A different bag, identified as Delaware and made in Oklahoma around 1850, combines glass beads, cloth, hide and ribbon. White outlines sharpen its bold geometric patterns. The museum places this work within artistic adaptation after removal; families carried design knowledge into new circumstances.

The 1737 Walking Purchase dispossessed Lenape communities in eastern Pennsylvania. Archival historians explain how an alleged land agreement was exploited through a prepared route and unusually fast walkers. A transaction presented as a measured walk became a means of taking far more land and pushing people west.

In September 1778, White Eyes, John Kill Buck and Captain Pipe negotiated a treaty with United States commissioners. Article III allowed troops to pass through Delaware country, promised payment for food and horses, and proposed a fort to protect families while warriors were away. Diplomacy concerned household safety as well as armies.

A small written sample in the community’s modern dictionary is “wanìshi”, meaning “Thank you!” The page provides audio and an example sentence. This is a present-day written teaching resource for Lenape, not a claim that this spelling appeared on an object from the map’s sixteenth-century interval.

Lenape people today belong to several distinct nations, including Delaware Nation and Delaware Tribe of Indians in Oklahoma, Stockbridge-Munsee in Wisconsin, and Munsee and Delaware First Nations in Ontario. Forced removals help explain this geography. Shared history and family ties coexist with separate governments.

ending.text: The map’s 1650 cutoff is not a disappearance. Later diplomacy, dispossession and removals reshaped Lenape life, while descendants maintain distinct nations, community institutions and language teaching.
